name: GhostHands
caption: visionOS simulator · authored paper-boat lesson
short: A hands-on lesson, placed right in front of you.
intro: GhostHands brings demonstrations out of a flat video and onto a real tabletop. Translucent hands, animated models, spoken instructions, and reference video share one spatial workspace on Apple Vision Pro.
built: A table-anchored workspace with animated paper-boat instructions and hand-joint recording and replay.
Interactive teaching models for engines, turbines, gears, brakes, pumps, cams, belts, and crank mechanisms.
Lesson authoring with written steps, video timestamps, fingertip-placed arrows, and importable lesson files.
Voice commands, offline narration, and an experimental iPhone-to-Apple Watch haptic relay.
why: Watching someone do a task is different from understanding where your own hands should go. GhostHands explores that gap by putting the demonstration where the work happens.
role: Built with Ethan Holm at SASEHacks. My work centered on the native spatial workspace, interaction, learning tools, mechanical labs, and companion-device experiments.
note: Submitted to SASEHacks. The images are simulator captures. Demonstrations are authored illustrations; arbitrary YouTube videos are not automatically converted to 3D. Watch feedback remains experimental.

name: Crank
caption: Actual Crank adaptation development capture · machinery and lift
short: An industrial horror game you operate with your hands.
intro: A native Apple Vision Pro adaptation of Crank It! that turns the game's machinery into a spatial interaction problem: a lift, physical controls, a CRT console, and the tension of working in a confined industrial space.
built: A themed three-dimensional CRT menu and equipment console, designed for mixed reality.
Physical, look-and-pinch, and hybrid controls with adjustable interaction settings.
Placement and seated/reclined calibration, spatial audio, and revised pause and return flows.
Iterations on the lift, crank, keyboard interactions, cables, collision, lighting, and lifecycle recovery.
why: A port becomes interesting when the original interaction is rethought for the device. Here, the challenge was making machinery feel usable with bare hands while preserving the game's atmosphere.
role: Native adaptation, spatial interface, control design, and integration work. Original Crank It! by James Dornan and Mike Klubnika; original game content retains its creators’ authorship.
note: Personal experimental adaptation, not an official release. Headset comfort and final interaction quality remain iterative. No game download is distributed here.
extraCaption: Original spatial CRT menu from the native adaptation

name: Wieman OS
caption: Original Wieman OS revenue interface · existing synthetic-data demo
short: One private console for an independent operator.
intro: Wieman OS brings the moving pieces of a service business into one workspace: clients, follow-ups, tasks, revenue, connected tools, and an AI copilot. It is designed to run in the owner's hosting and database accounts.
built: An operations overview connecting the client pipeline, daily priorities, and financial reporting.
Connections for supported email, calendar, billing, hosting, and AI services.
A contextual copilot with review and confirmation around sensitive actions.
A separate public demo using synthetic business records, plus a guided installation path.
why: Running a small business often means constantly switching between disconnected tools. The console gives the operator one place to regain context and decide what needs attention.
role: Product design, application development, integrations, public demo, and the installation experience.
note: The public demo uses sample data and responses. A production installation requires the owner's provider accounts and permissions.

name: POLY
caption: Spatial code map · visionOS simulator
short: Spread an idea around the room. Follow its connections.
intro: POLY explores spatial learning through connected code, anatomy, and other systems. Instead of flattening every relationship into a document, it gives the learner a map they can arrange, inspect, and follow.
built: A web study workspace and a native Vision Pro prototype with connected, movable source panes.
Code imports, dependency tracing, expandable readers, and grounded explanations.
Surround layouts, panel grips, resizing, and experiments with room-aware placement.
Learning flows for exploring, tracing, comparing, explaining, and pinning evidence.
why: Some ideas are easier to understand when their relationships stay visible. POLY asks what learning looks like when the room becomes the workspace.
role: Technical prototype and native Vision Pro development within a five-person OU project team.
note: Academic prototype. The submitted explanation engine used deterministic logic; it should not be mistaken for a general-purpose live AI tutor. Room placement and gesture comfort remain areas of iteration.

name: Stark Workshop & Hands
caption: Hand-armor render from the development project
short: A workshop, a heads-up display, and wearable digital tools.
intro: A set of Iron Man-inspired Vision Pro experiments combining an immersive workshop, holographic panels, calibrated hand armor, repulsor interactions, and a heads-up display.
built: A combined native experience for workshop, passthrough, hand fitting, and HUD experiments.
Hand calibration, articulated armor placement, and rigid/flexible material experiments.
Movable spatial panels, palm-based interaction, floor placement, and spatial sound.
why: This project is a test bed for interfaces that live around the body: what should follow your hands, what should stay in the room, and what should stay in view?
role: Native application, interaction experiments, hand calibration, rendering integration, and iteration from headset feedback.
note: Unofficial fan-inspired prototype, with third-party assets. It is not affiliated with Marvel or an official product. Visual fit, tracking latency, and comfort remain experimental.

name: Premier Fleet
short: Maintenance records that become a usable fleet workflow.
intro: A fleet-maintenance application built around the practical work of logging service, organizing equipment records, and turning scattered maintenance information into something a team can find and act on.
built: A purpose-built maintenance application with authenticated access and role-aware views.
Structured equipment and service records, reporting, and data-driven assistant experiments.
A workflow shaped around actual maintenance-entry requirements rather than a generic dashboard.
why: The useful system is the one that fits the daily user's work. This build focused on getting the maintenance workflow right before expanding the platform.
role: Application design, implementation, database and authentication integration, and prototype iteration.
note: Private prototype; not presented as an adopted production system. Customer records and internal documents are not included in this portfolio.
caption: Original fleet dashboard rendered locally · synthetic maintenance data

name: Pixler HQ
short: Rental operations, connected from arrival to checkout.
intro: A real-estate operations workspace exploring how stays, units, finances, connected devices, and an assistant can work together. The project includes an automation engine for check-in and checkout workflows.
built: A command center for units, stays, finance, settings, and automation history.
Integration adapters for payments, smart locks, thermostats, banking, and messaging.
Check-in/checkout logic, overlap checks, local-time scheduling, and a contextual assistant.
why: A rental workflow crosses both software and the physical world. The interesting engineering is making those transitions explicit, recoverable, and visible.
role: Application, interaction design, automation engine, integration architecture, and reliability work.
note: Prototype. Real hardware and third-party connections depend on configured accounts; a working interface is not a claim of a fully connected live property.
caption: Original rental command center rendered locally · synthetic stays

name: Shipping & Order Operations
short: From incoming orders to fulfillment and tracking.
intro: Operational software developed during my work with Plasma Bionics: an earlier WooCommerce-to-UPS shipping workflow, and a related order-management console for viewing orders, fulfillment, tracking, and customer links.
built: An order-to-fulfillment workflow linking WooCommerce orders with UPS shipping.
Automation around the repeated steps of preparing and processing outgoing orders.
A companion order-management interface with an open-order queue, shipment tracking, and links to customer organizations.
why: Re-entering the same information across systems creates work without adding value. This project connected the tools around the actual fulfillment process.
role: Shipping-service integration and operational workflow implementation, plus order-management interface development.
note: The image shows the related V20 order-management console rendered locally with synthetic orders. The earlier WooCommerce-to-UPS automation was a separate workflow with no standalone dashboard.
caption: Companion V20 order console · synthetic orders; separate from the earlier shipping script

name: V20 Device Platform
short: A bridge between embedded hardware and a fleet dashboard.
intro: A connected-device development effort spanning an Arduino Opta firmware port and a web platform for sterilizer telemetry, device state, manuals, and support workflows.
built: Firmware and interface work around an Arduino Opta-based controller.
A fleet dashboard for telemetry, cycle history, device configuration, and diagnostic views.
Customer-portal and assistant experiments grounded in device records and manuals.
why: Useful device software connects three perspectives: the controller's state, the service team's diagnosis, and the operator's next action.
role: Firmware port, dashboard and portal development, and device-to-cloud integration experiments.
note: Engineering prototype spanning firmware and web software. Hardware integration and real-device validation are separate from the dashboard demonstration.
caption: Original V20 fleet interface rendered locally · synthetic device telemetry

name: Covenant
short: Financial calculations in code. Explanations in plain language.
intro: A loan-package studio exploring how deterministic financial calculations can support an AI-assisted narrative. The key design choice was to keep the model from being the calculator.
built: A TypeScript engine for amortization, cash-flow projections, coverage ratios, and stress scenarios.
A workspace for inspecting a deal and its assumptions.
Narrative generation grounded in computed results, with a deterministic fallback.
why: An explanation is more useful when the numbers can be traced back to explicit calculations. The prototype separates calculation from prose generation.
role: Financial-engine prototype, interface, and narrative integration.
note: Archived prototype using sample cases and scripted intake. The calculation engine is implemented; some analytical assumptions remained open for further review.
caption: Original loan-modeling workspace · built-in sample deal
extraCaption: Five-year cash-flow projection in the original workspace · sample deal

name: Pioneer Timer
short: Cross-country timing that keeps working off the grid.
intro: An offline-first timing tool built for my dad's work with the Stillwater High School cross-country team. The interface is designed around the moments when a coach needs fast, readable timing rather than another account to manage.
built: An on-device progressive web app with runner timing and roster tools.
Shareable roster links and files, plus printable PDF results.
A compact, precision-instrument interface with stable, readable time displays.
why: A tool used beside a race should work where the race happens, even without a reliable connection.
role: Product design, offline application, roster sharing, and PDF generation.
note: Built as a family/team favor. The hosted app is access restricted. Rosters and results are stored on the device, with explicit sharing.
caption: Original timing interface rendered locally · fictional runners

name: Ghost Piston
short: A virtual engine, synthesized in the browser.
intro: A browser-based synthetic engine-sound experiment for an electric vehicle. Rather than looping a recording, it explores engine character through real-time audio synthesis and a driving-inspired interface.
built: A Web Audio synthesis engine with multiple engine presets and per-cylinder firing behavior.
GPS-driven input experiments, audio limiting, and a responsive visual HUD.
A self-contained application with an offline render harness for checking audio behavior.
why: Sound design becomes a systems problem when the sound has to respond continuously to changing input.
role: Application design, audio synthesis, browser interface, and signal-validation tooling.
note: Personal audio experiment. Browser and GPS behavior vary by device; it is not a vehicle control system.
caption: Original audio dashboard · local interface capture with audio and GPS disabled
extraCaption: Original engine-preset library · local interface capture

name: LibreQuake Hands
short: A classic shooter, rebuilt around controller-free interaction.
intro: A native immersive Vision Pro adaptation using LibreQuake content, with hand-driven movement and combat, spatial menus, campaign progress, and experiments that turn a scanned room into a play space.
built: Hand-only locomotion, aiming, jumping, and a physical axe interaction mode.
Immersive rendering, positional audio, campaign saves, and a three-dimensional map viewer.
Room Hunt experiments using scanned spaces for encounters and pickups.
why: The port explores how established game mechanics translate to hands, head movement, and the room around the player.
role: Native adaptation, hand controls, spatial menus, room-play experiments, and testing. Original engine and LibreQuake content retain their upstream authorship.
note: Experimental adaptation; local and simulator testing do not establish headset comfort or sustained performance. No game package is distributed here.
caption: Three-dimensional map viewer · visionOS simulator

name: Development Hub
short: Multiple spatial experiments. One consistent way in and out.
intro: A native host for several Vision Pro experiments, with a compact spatial launcher and shared conventions for entering, pausing, and leaving immersive experiences.
built: A minimal icon-based launch interface for integrated experiences.
Lifecycle integration across different native and game-engine components.
Shared attention to exit gestures, resource boundaries, saves, and return-to-menu behavior.
why: Integration is its own piece of engineering: several experiences need to coexist without leaving stale scenes, windows, audio, or input behind.
role: Host application and integration work across the spatial project collection.
note: A personal development environment, not a public app store or a way to redistribute third-party games.
caption: Native Development launcher · cropped visionOS simulator capture

name: A Restless Dream
caption: Development capture · native bedroom scene
short: A horror experience designed around a reclined viewpoint.
intro: A native Vision Pro adaptation of a sleep-paralysis horror experience, with particular attention to the player's reclined viewpoint, calibration, room-scale presentation, and the transition from menu into the scene.
built: Native immersive rendering and a spatial menu.
Reclined calibration, gaze-and-pinch confirmation, and revised gameplay controls.
Work on startup, scene loading, original-content integration, and menu lifecycle.
why: When the expected posture changes, the interface has to change with it. This project explores interaction and orientation from a bed or reclined position.
role: Native port and interface adaptation. The original game's story, scenes, and creative assets are not my original work.
note: Personal native adaptation with local development captures. Original game content retains its upstream authorship; the port is not publicly distributed.

name: Hunting Hands
short: A narrative game, translated into immersive hand controls.
intro: A native Vision Pro adaptation of Hunting by KitsuKell, exploring controller-free movement, rifle interaction, a scope, and narrative progression in an immersive scene.
built: A native Godot/visionOS runtime path with hand input and spatial menus.
Locomotion, aim/fire, scope controls, pickup/drop-off, and story transitions.
Tracking-loss input release, pause, replay, and host integration hooks.
why: The challenge is to preserve a game's sequence and atmosphere while replacing desktop input with spatial interaction.
role: Native adaptation and controls; original game by KitsuKell.
note: Personal experimental port. The standalone handoff was locally built and tested; physical Vision Pro behavior was not validated in that handoff. No game download is offered.
caption: Actual game-development capture · local desktop preview of the adaptation

name: Total Chaos AVP
short: A complex survival game, brought into a native headset runtime.
intro: An experimental Vision Pro adaptation of the free GZDoom edition of Total Chaos, spanning immersive rendering, hand controls, spatial menus, and the less visible work of inventory, saves, and lifecycle recovery.
built: A native GZDoom-to-visionOS runtime with stereo rendering and original audio integration.
Hand-driven combat, locomotion, inventory, crafting, journal, and save/load work.
A spatial map-case console and recovery paths for interrupted or failed sessions.
why: Getting a world to render is only the start. The project focused on preserving the supporting systems that make a long-form game playable.
role: Runtime port, spatial interface, control mapping, and targeted local verification. Original game, engine, and assets retain their upstream authorship.
note: Personal adaptation of the free GZDoom edition. Verification covered targeted local scenarios rather than a full campaign or complete headset playthrough. The port is not publicly distributed.
caption: Native rendering test from the adaptation · simulator eye capture

name: Buckshot Spatial Study
short: Tabletop tension as a spatial interaction experiment.
intro: A personal Vision Pro development study around a tabletop roulette-style game, using an existing community codebase to investigate a spatial menu, game presentation, and host integration.
built: Vision Pro integration experiments for an existing Godot game codebase.
Spatial menu and presentation work within the wider Development project.
why: A tabletop game provides a concrete setting for testing where a spatial interface should sit and how a player should interact with it.
role: Port and interface experimentation. Based on OpenBuckshotRoulette by 1503Dev; original Buckshot Roulette by Mike Klubnika.
note: Unofficial personal study. Original game rights remain with the creator; no source or game assets are distributed through this portfolio.
caption: Spatial game-menu development capture

name: WildWorld
short: Describe a habitat. Explore a living spatial world.
intro: A Vision Pro research project that turns a natural-language world request into a validated scene specification, then assembles a habitat with procedural environments and behavior-driven creatures.
built: A structured world specification and native RealityKit scene architecture.
Procedural pipelines for vegetation, environments, creatures, and ambient sound.
Behavior models and validation tooling to keep generated content within explicit contracts.
why: Generated worlds need more than a compelling prompt. The project explores the structure, asset pipeline, and behavior rules that make a requested environment coherent.
role: Application architecture, procedural asset tooling, and world-generation experiments.
note: Research prototype with stylized placeholder creatures. Photorealism and fully verified headset behavior are not claimed.
caption: Procedural creature proof render from the original asset pipeline
extraCaption: Environment texture and vegetation proofs from the original procedural asset pipeline

name: OU After Dark
caption: In-game development capture · stylized OU campus
short: A familiar campus, reimagined after hours.
intro: A survival-game prototype set in a stylized interpretation of the University of Oklahoma campus, combining recognizable landmarks, exploration, encounters, and extraction-style objectives.
built: A campus world with mapped exterior buildings and enterable landmark interiors.
Story and encounter flows, inventory and weapons, voiced scenes, and adjustable audio.
Save/checkpoint behavior, map navigation, difficulty settings, and a packaged desktop build.
why: This project combines world-building with the practical systems behind a playable game: progression, readable objectives, recoverable sessions, and a coherent sense of place.
role: Game implementation, campus-world assembly, interface, and iterative playability work.
note: Independent student game prototype. Campus and characters are stylized; it is not an official OU product or an exact digital replica.

name: Apex Custom Innovations
short: An automotive website with the finish of a custom build.
intro: A premium website concept for an automotive customization shop, built around a sharp, restrained layout, strong photography, service discovery, and a clear route to an inquiry.
built: A responsive single-page website with an automotive visual identity.
Service sections, a gallery, location information, and a quote-composer flow.
Keyboard, mobile, security-header, and interaction refinements.
why: The design aims to let the craftsmanship carry the page, with the interface giving the work room to speak.
role: Website design and implementation as a prospect concept.
note: An uncommissioned concept, not the company's adopted website or evidence of a client relationship. Photography and brand assets belong to Apex.
caption: Apex website concept · browser capture

name: Wieman Systems & Personal Brand
short: A clear digital home for the work and the person behind it.
intro: The Wieman Systems website and my personal brand site communicate the same approach from two perspectives: the systems I build and the person accountable for building them.
built: A monochrome visual system with architectural typography, restrained motion, and responsive layouts.
Service and product pages, contact flows, and a dedicated portfolio.
Performance-minded static pages and consistent navigation across the personal site.
why: A business website should make the work understandable and make the next step obvious.
role: Design, development, content, and ongoing iteration.
note: The personal site is this portfolio's home. The business site includes the Wieman OS product showcase.
caption: Personal brand homepage · browser capture

name: Email & Productivity Agents
short: A second pass over the busywork, with a person in control.
intro: A collection of internal tools exploring inbox triage, drafting, follow-up awareness, and the small recurring tasks that otherwise disappear between work sessions.
built: Email-watch and action-item tooling.
Context-aware drafting and follow-up workflows.
Integration experiments connecting the inbox with an operations workspace.
why: The value of an agent is often in remembering the small things reliably, then giving the operator enough context to make the decision.
role: Workflow design, integrations, and internal tooling.
note: The screenshot shows inbox actions in the related Wieman OS console using its synthetic-data demo. Earlier email-watch tools ran separately; the image does not establish that a historical agent is currently running.
caption: Wieman OS inbox actions · existing synthetic-data demo

name: Client Delivery Toolkit
short: The foundation underneath a repeatable client delivery.
intro: Reusable starting points and delivery tools for client projects: brochure and application starters, onboarding workflows, branded setup materials, and operational utilities.
built: Static-site and full-stack application starters with shared design and security conventions.
Onboarding forms, client setup guides, invoice tooling, and reusable delivery workflows.
Project checks and integration patterns that reduce repeated setup work.
why: Good foundations let the next project spend more time on the client's actual problem.
role: Tooling, templates, workflow design, and ongoing refinement.
note: The original setup-guide template is shown with an example client and account-specific fields removed. This internal toolkit supports the wider project collection.
